newsitem.title: USA: Analysts cut AT&T 1997 estimates on weak Q1.
newsitem.headline: Analysts cut AT&T 1997 estimates on weak Q1.

text.p: AT&T Corp produced even weaker than expected results in the first quarter, analysts say. While earnings per share of $0.69 versus $0.85 a year ago matched First Call estimates, a deeper dig shows weaknesses.
Most of those polled so far expect to lower their 1997 earnings estimates by at least $0.10 per share.

"We will probably lower our 1997 results because of a combination of a lower than expected first quarter and higher than forecast spending on new initiatives," said analyst Bette Massick of brokerage Bear Stearns.
Massick said she was lowering her forecast of $2.75 for 1997, probably to $2.65, but would keep the neutral rating she has for the stock.
"I expect others are going to (cut their ratings) as well," she said.

"The evidence in the quarter is that they are giving away a lot more minutes than we thought, diluting earnings more than we thought, and core earnings are growing more slowly than we thought," said Richard Klugman of Goldman Sachs.
AT&T told a conference call on Monday that second quarter results were likely to be a little weaker than the first's, but it remained committed to its broad earnings targets for 1997.

AT&T told analysts in March it expected to make between $2.45 and $3.00 for 1997, including investment costs for new markets of between $0.75 and $1 per share. It said on Monday it now expects those costs to be nearer $1 than $0.75.
"There was not a great deal to cheer in the results," Klugman said, adding that he was likely to cut his estimate for earnings per share for the year from the current $2.70.
AT&T made $3.66 in net earnings per share in 1996.
Klugman noted some bright spots were an improvement in the credit card business and good growth in the volume of calls on AT&T's network business.
Wireless, the fastest growing division in AT&T, is still not quite keeping up with the whole market, analysts said.

"They said they were seeing pricing pressure and pressure on subscriber (growth) from new entrants," said Barry Sine, an analyst at SBC Warburg. Advertising and marketing costs were also higher than expected.
"The new wireless operations will be net-income negative for some time to come," Sine said.

No analysts polled said they were changing their investment rating on the stock, and some said the shares had already taken aboard a full measure of pessimism about the company over the last few months.
At 1330 EDT/1730 GMT AT&T stock was down 1/2 at 33-1/4.
Robert Wilkes of Brown Brothers Harriman was sanguine that the company was meeting its own yardsticks for change in a very trying environment.
"Potentially the second quarter should be the low point of the year," Wilkes said. He noted that the new strategies had only been driven hard in the month since the analysts' meeting.
"After all, you don't turn an aircraft carrier like AT&T around in a month," Wilkes said. (( New York Newsroom 212 859 1712))
